text: State, step, stop: worked simulation problems.
Read every rule State variables Step apply rules Output exact format repeat

A simulation problem has no clever trick: the difficulty is reading every rule correctly and turning it into code without slips. Decide the state (which variables describe the situation), the step (how one event changes it), and the stop condition.
Checklist before coding: list every rule from the statement; note edge cases (empty input, ties, wrap-around); check the output format character by character.
Most wrong answers here are misread rules, not bad algorithms.
WWWWWWWWWWWW LE
State: the two scores of the current game. Step: one character. Stop: a game ends when one side reaches the target and leads by 2; the input ends at 'E' .

Number the seats 0 … n−1. Moving s seats round a circle is (p + s) % n one way and (p - s + n) % n the other.
Facing in or out flips left and right. Instead of four cases, notice that "facing direction equals instruction" always means the same way round: one comparison decides it (P1563).
p - s can be negative and % keeps the sign: add n first. If s can exceed n, reduce it with s % n .
Copy a rule table from the statement into a 2D array once, then every round is a lookup instead of a chain of if s (P1328).
A pattern of length k that repeats forever: round i uses element i % k .

Grid simulations (P2670 minesweeper, P4924 rotating sub-squares, P1518 two walkers) reuse the 入门 4 tools: dx/dy arrays, bounds checks, rotate into a second array. When a walk might never end, stop after a safe maximum number of steps or detect a repeated state.
Split the output into small decisions, one per rule: sign, coefficient, variable, power. Each decision is one if that matches one sentence of the statement (P1067).

text: String expansion (P1098) and work scheduling (P1065) are the same style: many small rules, each a separate, testable piece.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide numbers stored digit by digit.
987 + 45: 7+5=12 → 2 carry 1; 8+4+1=13 → 3 carry 1; 9+0+1=10 → 0 carry 1; last carry → new digit 1 result d = 2 3 0 1 → printed backwards: 1032
long long stops at about 9.2 × 1018. Longer numbers are kept as a vector of digits, ones digit first. Then digit i of every number lines up at index i, and a carry simply moves to index i + 1.

Every operation is the school method: work from the ones digit up, keep a carry (or borrow), and remove leading zeros at the end. // a big number: digits stored backwards, d[0] = ones digit vector<int> toBig(const string &s) { vector<int> d; for (int i = int(s.size()) - 1; i >= 0; i--) d.push_back(s[i] - '0'); return d; } void trim(vector<int> &d) { // drop leading zeros, keep one digit while (d.size() > 1 && d.back() == 0) d.pop_back(); } void print(const vector<int> &d) { for (int i = int(d.size()) - 1; i >= 0; i--) cout << d[i]; cout << "\n"; }
Read the number as a string , convert with toBig , compute, trim , then print from the last index down. Every program below starts with these three helpers.
Loop while there are digits left in either number or a carry. Each step: digit sum + carry; keep % 10 , pass / 10 on (P1601).
Numbers of different lengths need no padding: a missing digit counts as 0.
Compare first: more digits means bigger; equal length → compare from the highest digit down. Subtract the smaller from the larger and put a minus sign in front if you swapped.
Borrow: when a digit goes negative, add 10 and take 1 from the next digit. trim afterwards, so 1000 − 999 prints 1, not 0001.

title: Multiplying by a small number, and factorials

text: Multiplying by an ordinary int k touches each digit once: digit × k + carry . The final carry can be several digits long, so push them one by one.
n! for n up to 1000 has about 2568 digits; this loop handles it easily. Counting how often a digit appears in n! is then a tally over f (P1591).
digit * k + carry must fit in an int : fine for k up to about 108. For bigger k use long long or big × big multiplication.
Combine the pieces: keep the running factorial f and the running sum. Each round is one small multiplication and one big addition (P1009, the problem from 入门 3 that needed this list).
Build each new value from the previous one (k! = (k−1)! × k) instead of recomputing from scratch. The same habit makes 2p cheap (P1045).
a[i] × b[j] adds into c[i + j]

Digit i of a times digit j of b lands in column i + j. Add all products first (in long long ), then sweep the carries once. A result has at most len(a) + len(b) digits; trim removes the rest, so 0 × 12345 prints 0 (P1303). Cost: O(len(a) × len(b)).
Long division goes the other way, from the highest digit down: bring down one digit into the remainder, write the quotient digit, keep the remainder.

Only the remainder is needed for "is this huge number divisible by k?" questions. The last 500 digits of a power (P1045) are a big multiplication that throws away everything above digit 500; the digit count of 2p is ⌊p · log102⌋ + 1.

P1249: split n into distinct parts 2, 3, 4, … and adjust the last ones, then multiply the parts with mulSmall . C C LANGUAGE · ADDITIONAL INFORMATION Classic C solutions store big numbers in fixed int arrays with a separate length, read the digits into a char array with scanf("%s") , clear arrays with memset , and use strlen for the length. The arithmetic is the same column method.
A fixed array must be large enough for the longest answer (len(a) + len(b) + 1 digits for a product). A vector grows by itself.

Key points to memorise
1. Simulation: list every rule, choose the state, write one step, know when to stop.
2. Check the output format character by character; most errors are misread rules.
3. Circle of n: (p + s) % n and (p - s % n + n) % n.
4. Rule tables go into a 2D array; repeating patterns use i % k.
5. Formatting: one small if per rule (sign, 1, x, power, first term).
6. Endless walks: cap the steps or detect a repeated state.
7. Big numbers: vector<int> of digits, ones digit first; read as a string.
8. Add: digit + digit + carry, keep % 10, pass / 10; loop while digits or carry remain.
9. Compare by length, then from the top digit; subtract smaller from larger and add "−".
10. Borrow: +10 here, −1 at the next digit; always trim leading zeros.
11. Big × small: digit × k + carry; push the final carry digit by digit.
12. Big × big: c[i + j] += a[i] * b[j], then one carry sweep.
13. Big ÷ small: from the top digit down, rem = rem × 10 + digit.
14. (C) Fixed int arrays + char input + memset + strlen do the same job; size them for the longest answer.
